cards.definition: Direct communication between paid representatives and prospects that leads to transactions, customer satisfaction, account development, and profitable relationships.
Management of the field sales operation; it turns personal selling into a managed process aligned with organizational goals.

cards.term: Sales management in the marketing mix
cards.definition: Sales management falls under Promotion. Its major responsibilities include planning and budgeting, recruiting and selecting, training, motivating and compensating, designing territories, and evaluating performance.
The knowledge, skills, behaviors, and attitudes needed to perform effectively.

Global competition, shorter product cycles, and blurred boundaries give customers more power and higher expectations while pushing sellers toward solutions, teams, inside selling, and productivity measures.
Understand their business, support their interests, design suitable applications, remain accessible, solve problems, respond creatively, and accept accountability for results.
A short-term approach emphasizing sales skills, products, price, service, and immediate revenue.
A collaborative approach emphasizing management skills, customer solutions, differentiation through people, customer lifetime value, and trusted-advisor status.
Transactional selling focuses on short-term product, price, and revenue; relationship selling focuses on collaborative solutions, people-based differentiation, and customer lifetime value.
Lead by example, model professional conduct, and share best practices.
Use open two-way communication, collaboration, creativity, initiative, and appropriate risk taking.
Create a supportive structure, reward fairly, align team and organizational goals, hire and train for teamwork, and use each member's strengths.
Knowing one's goals, values, strengths, and weaknesses; learning from experience; and remaining willing to unlearn and relearn.
Understanding desired outcomes, adapting management practices, and encouraging the sales force to accept and use appropriate selling technology.
A salesperson tries to win the next customer; a sales manager builds a repeatable system by managing people, processes, and performance.
The process of creating and sustaining competitive advantage.
A statement that provides direction and defines the firm's potential.
Customers, competitors, and the company; together they define the basic character of the business.
Specific, measurable objectives expressed through profit, revenue, unit sales, market share, survival, or social responsibility and communicated throughout the organization.
Strategy provides the direction for reaching objectives; tactics are the specific actions used to carry out that strategy.
Integrated decisions and actions used to achieve marketing objectives by addressing customer value requirements.
Sales objectives align from corporate goals to business-unit, marketing, sales-department, district, salesperson, and major-account objectives.
A group of customers with common characteristics, similar needs, and similar responses to a marketing program.
Selecting and prioritizing the market segments the company will pursue.
Segment customers by the attraction and retention activities they require, identify the essential activities and participants for each segment, and decide when face-to-face selling is justified.
A direct sales force, agents, distributors, retailers, integrators, alliances, advertising, promotion, direct mail, telemarketing, and the Internet can all help reach customers.
Lower-cost channels provide efficiency; a sales force costs more but offers greater personal effectiveness.
Go-to-market strategy, product development management, supply chain management, and customer relationship management.
The strategy-implementation process that addresses customer access.
The strategy-implementation process that creates and improves offerings.

Integration of information and logistics across firms to create and deliver customer value, including supplier relationships, logistics, production, channel partners, orders, pricing, installation, and maintenance.
A comprehensive set of processes and technologies for managing relationships with prospects, customers, and business partners across marketing, sales, and service, regardless of channel.
A plan for how the sales force will contribute to company objectives.
Choosing the right customers and the right relationship type; the choice is strategic for both supplier and customer.
An account relationship emphasizing acceptable quality, competitive price, and convenience.
An account relationship that creates value beyond the product.
An account relationship that uses the supplier's corporate assets to advance the customer's strategic success.

cards.term: Transactional vs. consultative vs. enterprise accounts
cards.definition: Transactional accounts seek a convenient product exchange; consultative accounts seek added value beyond the product; enterprise accounts use the supplier's full corporate assets for the customer's strategy.
Acquire new customers, retain current customers, and increase each customer's profitable purchases.
A description of a promising prospect using factors such as demographics, business size, product-line age, geographic distance, and need for a product-line specialist.
Cold canvassing, direct mail, trade shows, directories, the Internet, and referrals from existing customers.
Evaluating the prospect's need, buying authority, and ability to pay so salespeople do not overinvest in weak opportunities.
Build long-term loyalty while allocating selling resources carefully; consultative relationships require more time than transactional relationships.
The allocation of time, compensation, and other direct selling expenses to a sales call.
The sales volume required to cover direct selling expenses.
A call-allocation model using several customer characteristics, often sales volume, sales potential, and gross margin; it fits consultative selling.
A call-allocation model based on customer response over time; it is more likely in transactional selling.
The portfolio model uses multiple customer characteristics to guide calls in consultative selling; the decision model uses customer response over time to guide calls in transactional selling.
A way to sort opportunities by their probability of becoming sales: unqualified opportunities, qualified opportunities, and the best few opportunities.
What the customer pays minus the cost of servicing the account.
The sum of a customer's expected future profit contributions.

cards.term: Sales vs. profit vs. customer lifetime value
cards.definition: Sales are revenue received; profit is revenue less account-service costs; customer lifetime value is the customer's expected future profit contribution.
Eliminate distractions, set goals, make a list, complete items, and transfer unfinished priorities forward.
Everyone formally or informally involved in a purchase decision, including people who approve the purchase and people who influence the final decision.
Identify all buying influences and understand what matters to each instead of focusing only on the first contact or the person who places the order.
The buying influence that asks whether the purchase benefits the business over the long term.
The buying influence that considers how the purchase will affect the job or work.
The buying influence that checks specifications and requirements.
The buying influence that wants the salesperson and proposed solution to succeed.
Membership varies with the purchase, departments involved, dollar value, and technical sophistication.
A supporter may like the product without controlling the budget or final approval.
A routine repurchase with little or no change.
A repeat purchase in which the buyer considers changes to specifications, suppliers, price, or terms.
Awareness, exploration, expansion, commitment, and dissolution. The stages are dynamic and do not always proceed in a perfectly linear order.
Create value, meet expectations, and build trust; strong relationships require all three.

cards.term: Components of trust in sales relationships
cards.definition: Competence, dependability, customer orientation, likability, and honesty.
Honesty is the most critical component emphasized in the Exam 1 guide.
Names of potential prospects provided by satisfied customers, connecting relationship quality with opportunity development.
Ask questions first to understand customer needs and the current purchase stage before arguing that your product is better.
When a contact lacks budget authority, identify the other people involved in the decision instead of continuing to persuade only that contact.
Learn what matters to the customer, meet expectations consistently, and keep finding ways to provide additional value.
Pre-interaction, interaction, and post-interaction.
Planning before meeting decision makers.
Relating, discovery, advocacy, objection handling, and closing.
Support and follow-through after the transaction.
Uses prepared statements about an offering to stimulate a positive response.
Translating a product feature into a competitive advantage connected to a customer benefit.
Discovers and meets customer needs by identifying likely buyers, creating an incentive to change, building confidence to invest, and ensuring fulfillment of value promises.
Uses a formal study of the customer's operations, followed by a written proposal and often a team presentation; it fits complex, expensive purchases with longer selling cycles.
Standardized selling uses prepared benefit statements; need-satisfaction selling discovers customer needs; problem-solution selling uses a formal operational study and proposal.
What do I want to accomplish? What do I know about the customer? Where can I find the information? What will I say? Accurate details, including the customer's name, matter.
Gaining access, relating to the customer, discovering needs, advocating a solution, and recognizing when to close.
Offering additional products or services.
Moving the customer to a larger product or enhanced service.
Cross-selling adds products or services; upselling moves the customer to a larger product or enhanced service.
Recording what the salesperson learned about a prospect or customer, then analyzing successful and unsuccessful calls to shape future behavior.
Remain ethical and consistent while recognizing individual needs; managers should explain decisions clearly and balance organizational requirements with employee circumstances.
Effective selling focuses less on convincing people and more on understanding how buyers think, uncovering problems, and creating value.
Do not lead with an immediate product speech; ask purposeful questions, listen carefully, and understand the customer's situation before recommending anything.

cards.term: Why a clear no can help (Marc Wayshak)
cards.definition: It can reveal poor fit, conserve the salesperson's time, and shift effort toward qualified prospects instead of creating opportunity cost by chasing everyone.
Let the customer describe the problem, ask diagnostic questions, identify the underlying need, and recommend an appropriate solution.

cards.term: What to do instead of immediately pitching (Marc Wayshak)
cards.definition: Lead with questions, listening, and diagnosis so the recommendation addresses the prospect's actual needs.
Approach goals with competitive preparation, personal accountability, and an expectation that strong effort should produce measurable results.
Show measurable results rather than merely listing responsibilities because results demonstrate impact and provide evidence of performance.

cards.term: Equipped and paid to win (Julia Jordan)
cards.definition: Evaluate whether an employer provides the tools, training, leadership, and opportunity needed to succeed and whether compensation rewards the results the role expects.

cards.term: Career fair as a sales process (Julia Jordan)
cards.definition: Sell your value, clarify the next step before leaving, and obtain the recruiter's preferred contact information or permission to follow up.
Culture, purpose rather than passion, and professional and financial growth.

cards.term: Evaluating culture, purpose, and growth (Julia Jordan)
cards.definition: Culture shapes daily fit and leadership environment; purpose connects work to meaningful contribution; growth determines whether the role builds skills, responsibility, advancement, and earnings.
